source: Solar and Sidereal Days
Earth spins once in 23 h 56 min, but noon to noon takes 24 h because Earth also moves along its orbit.
Students think one day is exactly one full spin of Earth.
A day seems simple: Earth spins once. But "once" relative to what? On the celestial sphere there are two choices, the Sun and the distant stars, and they give two different days.

While Earth spins, it also moves along its orbit, about $360^\circ \div 365.25 \approx 1^\circ$ per day, in the same direction as it spins. After one full $360^\circ$ turn the stars are back where they were, but the Sun now lies about $1^\circ$ farther east among them. Earth must turn that extra $1^\circ$ to bring the Sun back to the meridian. At $15^\circ$ per hour, $1^\circ$ takes about 4 minutes, so a solar day is about 4 minutes longer than a sidereal day. In rates: $\dfrac{1}{\text{sidereal day}} = \dfrac{1}{\text{solar day}} + \dfrac{1}{\text{year}}$.

A sidereal day (one spin relative to the stars) is 23 h 56 min; a solar day (noon to noon) is 24 h, because Earth also moves about $1^\circ$ along its orbit each day and must turn about $361^\circ$ to face the Sun again.

Worked examples
Orion's bright star Rigel rises at 11:00 pm tonight. About when will it rise 30 days from now?
Stars rise earlier
About 9:00 pm.
Each night a star rises about 4 minutes earlier, because the clock keeps solar days and the star keeps sidereal days.
$30 \times 4 = 120$ min $= 2$ h earlier.
So about 9:00 pm. That is why the evening sky changes with the seasons.
How many times does Earth turn relative to the stars in one year?
Count the spins
In $365.25$ solar days the Sun appears to go once around the sky relative to the stars.
That means Earth makes one more turn relative to the stars than relative to the Sun.
$365.25 + 1 = 366.25$ sidereal days per year.

"A day is one spin of Earth" is only true for the sidereal day. From noon to noon Earth turns about $361^\circ$, not $360^\circ$. Check with the numbers: $366.25$ sidereal days of $23.934$ h make $8766$ h, the same as $365.25$ solar days of $24$ h.

Astronomers set their telescopes by sidereal time, because a star crosses the meridian at the same sidereal time every day: the sidereal time equals the right ascension on your meridian (see right ascension).
